claims.text: Corrosion-related degradation or retention of protection in Q235 steel during aggressive salt exposure at 700–900 °C is governed by the formation and stability of a protective oxide layer.
The microstructure of Q235 steel influences the formation and stability of its protective oxide layer.
Alloying elements in Q235 steel influence the formation and stability of its protective oxide layer.
Annealing Q235 steel before salt exposure enhances oxide-layer uniformity.
Annealing Q235 steel before salt exposure enhances oxide-layer adherence.
A more uniform and adherent oxide layer reduces mass change during high-temperature salt exposure.
A more uniform and adherent oxide layer improves the thermal stability of Q235 steel during high-temperature salt exposure.
Annealing modifies the microstructure of Q235 steel.
The annealing-induced microstructural modification promotes formation of a more uniform oxide layer during high-temperature salt exposure.
The annealing-induced microstructural modification promotes formation of a more adherent oxide layer during high-temperature salt exposure.
The oxide layer acts as a barrier to further oxidation and corrosion.
Annealed Q235 steel will show reduced mass change relative to non-annealed Q235 steel under otherwise identical high-temperature salt exposure.
Annealed Q235 steel will retain greater hardness than non-annealed Q235 steel under otherwise identical high-temperature salt exposure.
Annealed Q235 steel will show better thermal stability than non-annealed Q235 steel under otherwise identical high-temperature salt exposure.
Excessive annealing temperature or duration may cause grain coarsening and prevent the proposed protection mechanism from applying.
Salt environments containing species that disrupt oxide-layer formation may prevent the proposed protection mechanism from applying.
